generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, reflection is built into how you learn to be a psychologist. After a lab report, a practical, or a placement, you are expected to look back and ask not just what you found but how you worked: what your reasoning was, where it held up, and what you would do differently. A psychology degree treats this honest looking-back as part of becoming a competent, self-aware practitioner, not an optional extra.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students who have just had the same lab report returned with a middling mark and some feedback.

Tom reads the feedback, notes that the mark was lower than hoped, and writes: 'I got 58. The marker said my discussion was thin and my stats reporting was off. I will try harder next time.' This records what happened and ends with a vague intention. It is a description, not a reflection: it does not ask why the discussion was thin or what 'trying harder' would actually involve.

Amara reads the same feedback and looks back honestly. 'My discussion was thin because I described the results but never linked them back to the hypotheses or the wider literature. The stats reporting slipped because I rushed the formatting at the end. Next time I will draft the discussion around each hypothesis, and format the statistics as I write them up.' This is reflection: it asks why things went as they did and turns that into specific, doable changes.

Both students looked back at the same report. Only Amara moved past describing it to learning from it.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, reflection is a deliberate, honest look back at your work, a lab report, a practical, a placement, so that you can learn from it, not just a description of what happened. You can now explain what reflection is, recognise it in how a student looks back on their work, and say why it matters: it is how a self-regulating psychologist turns experience into improvement. The next lesson gives you a simple model for doing it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's log a reflection rather than a description?

items.text: She asked why her discussion and stats fell short, and turned it into specific changes.
She recorded her mark and the marker's comments accurately.
She wrote more than Tom did.
She promised to try harder next time.

feedback.correct: That's right. Asking why things fell short and planning specific changes is what makes it a reflection.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID beyond recording the feedback.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara reflected because she asked why her work fell short and planned specific changes, not because she recorded the feedback accurately or wrote more.
